JUDGE channel — VII. The frame experiment

Similarity, difference, and rgb’s conditional — does JUDGE behave like a contrast model or like a conditional probability?

ecb

2026-07-28

Design

Report VI read the JUDGE asymmetry as Tversky’s contrast model and got a good fit — half the directional variance is a single per-adjective prominence potential, the direction is right for 97% of high-gap pairs, and prominence separates cleanly from base rate and from lexical frequency. But two things were left standing.

  1. Everything was a statement about (β − α)f. The focusing weights are not separately identified by data collected in one frame.
  2. The whole reading assumed B[i,j] is a similarity judgment. rgb’s item is a conditional — “a person who is very i: how likely also j?” — and the deflationary rival is that it is simply P(j | i), in which case Tversky is the wrong theory and the prominence scale is a base rate wearing a costume.

This experiment holds the pair fixed and varies the question. 252 pairs × 3 frames × 2 orders = 1,512 prompts per model, on the four cohort models reachable on the Orin.

frame prompt polarity
cond Consider a person who is very a. How likely is this person to also be b? alikeness
sim How similar is a person who is very a to a person who is very b? alikeness
diff How different is a person who is very a from a person who is very b? differentness

Same 1–7 instruction and same system message in all three, so a frame effect cannot come from the response format. The grammatical subject is Tversky’s subject role; running both orders is the focusing manipulation. Pairs are stratified 2 × 3 on prominence gap (top vs bottom decile of |f_i − f_j|, using the f recovered in Report VI §2 from all 273,006 archival cells) × similarity tercile, so that common-feature mass and distinctive-feature mass vary as independently as this item pool allows.

What separates the two accounts. With c = f(A∩B), u = f(A−B), v = f(B−A): s = θc − αu − βv and d = α'u + β'v − θ'c, so Δs = (β−α)(u−v) and Δd = (α'−β')(u−v). The raw sign therefore flips between frames — but so does any reverse-scored measure, so the sign flip is not diagnostic (Report VI §8.2 states this correction). The tests that do discriminate:

  • T1 non-complementarity (primary). s + d = (θ−θ')c + (α'−α)u + (β'−β)v. If diff is just sim reverse-scored, the sum is constant. Under the contrast model it moves with the pair’s feature richness.
  • T2 asymmetry-to-signal ratio by frame. Distinctive features weigh more in difference judgments, so the relative asymmetry should be larger in diff. Pure polarity reversal predicts equality.
  • T3 frame-invariance of f. The archival prominence scale should predict the directional asymmetry in both new frames — genuine out-of-sample validation, which Report VI §2’s sign test explicitly was not.
  • T4 is cond a similarity judgment at all? The assumption Report VI granted itself.
tid <- read_csv_("frames_tidy.csv") %>% as_tibble()
FR  <- c("cond","sim","diff")
tid <- tid %>% mutate(frame = factor(frame, levels = FR))
ALLMOD <- sort(unique(tid$model))

1. Data quality first — one rater has to go

The primary measure is the digit the model actually emitted, not the logprob EV. That choice is forced. At temperature 0 the emitted token is the answer, but this endpoint’s top_logprobs are not always the distribution that produced it: qwen2.5:3b emits “5” on cells where the reported distribution puts 0.80 on “7”, and the disagreement rate reaches 61% on phi4-mini. This is a finding the whole track needs — the soft-evidence programme assumes those distributions are trustworthy, and on this endpoint, for some models, they are not.

tid %>% group_by(model, frame) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), `digit rate` = mean(text_ok),
            `logprob agrees with text` = mean(lp_agree, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean = mean(rating), sd = sd(rating), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.,3))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Response quality by model and frame. `digit rate` counts prompts that produced a parsable 1-7 at all.")

phi4-mini is excluded from every test below, for three independent reasons:

  1. Frame-differential non-response. It opens with prose (“I cannot provide an accurate answer…”) on 16.5% of sim prompts versus ~4% of cond and diff. Missingness that depends on the manipulation is exactly what a frame contrast cannot tolerate.
  2. The repair changes the answer. Seeding an assistant "Number:" turn does raise its digit rate, but it also moves its ratings — blind/thinking goes from 6 unprefilled to 2 prefilled. That is a different measurement, not a reformatted one.
  3. Degenerate diff responding. Its diff ratings have SD = 0.05 — it answers 6 to essentially every difference item.

Its refusal pattern is itself worth recording: the model balks specifically at the similarity frame, not at the conditional or the difference frame. llama3.2:3b is retained but is the known flat rater (SD 0.33–0.61), so it contributes little differentiated signal; the weight falls on the Gemmas and qwen2.5:3b.

tid <- tid %>% filter(model != "phi4-mini-latest")
MOD <- sort(unique(tid$model))
cat(sprintf("%d records | %d raters | %d pairs\n",
            nrow(tid), length(MOD), n_distinct(paste(tid$i, tid$j))))
## 7515 records | 5 raters | 252 pairs

2. Manipulation check

ggplot(tid, aes(rating, colour = frame)) + geom_density(linewidth = 0.7, adjust = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~model, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(cond = "#4C72B0", sim = "#55A868", diff = "#C44E52")) +
  labs(title = "The frames elicit different response distributions",
       x = "rating (raw polarity)", y = NULL) + theme_judge()

3. T4 — is rgb’s conditional a similarity judgment?

Pair-level correspondence between the frames, averaging the two orders (so this is about the symmetric signal, not the asymmetry):

wide <- tid %>% group_by(model, i, j, frame) %>% summarise(r = mean(rating), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = frame, values_from = r) %>%
  filter(!is.na(cond), !is.na(sim), !is.na(diff)) %>%   # complete pairs only
  mutate(diff_alike = 8 - diff)
arch <- {
  sym <- fread_gz("sym_ev.csv.gz"); disc <- setdiff(MODELS, c("Llama","FalconMamba"))
  S <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(disc, function(m) build_matrix(sym, m, "sym")))/length(disc)
  pr <- read_csv_("frame_pairs.csv") %>% as_tibble()
  pr %>% mutate(arch_sym = S[cbind(i+1L, j+1L)]) %>% select(i, j, arch_sym, gap, sym_design = sym,
                                                            f_i, f_j, block)
}
wide <- wide %>% left_join(arch, by = c("i","j"))
wide %>% group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(`cond ~ sim` = cor(cond, sim),
            `cond ~ reverse(diff)` = cor(cond, diff_alike),
            `sim ~ reverse(diff)`  = cor(sim, diff_alike),
            `cond ~ archival B` = cor(cond, arch_sym),
            `sim ~ archival B`  = cor(sim, arch_sym), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.,3))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Do the frames measure the same thing? (pair level, orders averaged). The archival column also validates this harness against rgb's original collection.")

4. T1 — non-complementarity (the primary test)

If diff is sim with the polarity reversed, sim + diff is a constant. Under the contrast model it varies with how much feature mass the pair has to work with.

nc <- wide %>% mutate(sum_sd = sim + diff, rich = f_i + f_j)
nc %>% group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(`mean(sim+diff)` = mean(sum_sd), `SD(sim+diff)` = sd(sum_sd),
            `r with overlap (archival B)` = cor(sum_sd, arch_sym),
            `r with richness (f_i+f_j)` = cor(sum_sd, rich), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.,3))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "T1: is sim + diff constant? A polarity-reversal account says SD ~ 0 and both correlations ~ 0.")
T1: is sim + diff constant? A polarity-reversal account says SD ~ 0 and both correlations ~ 0.
model mean(sim+diff) SD(sim+diff) r with overlap (archival B) r with richness (f_i+f_j)

map_dfr(MOD, function(m) {
  d <- nc %>% filter(model == m)
  if (nrow(d) < 10) return(tibble())
  fit <- lm(sum_sd ~ scale(arch_sym) + scale(rich), d)
  tibble(Model = m, n = nrow(d), `R²` = summary(fit)$r.squared,
         `b(overlap)` = coef(fit)[[2]], `t(overlap)` = summary(fit)$coefficients[2,3],
         `b(richness)` = coef(fit)[[3]], `t(richness)` = summary(fit)$coefficients[3,3])
}) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.,3))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "T1 regression: sim + diff on standardized overlap and richness.")

5. T3 — does the archival prominence scale predict the new frames?

For each frame, the directional asymmetry on the alikeness polarity, Δ = r(i→j) − r(j→i), regressed on the archival prominence difference f_i − f_j. Report VI predicts a negative slope in every frame (the less prominent adjective is the better subject).

asym <- tid %>%
  mutate(val = rating_alike) %>%
  select(model, i, j, frame, order, val) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = order, values_from = val) %>%
  filter(!is.na(ij), !is.na(ji)) %>%          # both orders needed for a delta
  mutate(delta = ij - ji) %>%
  left_join(arch, by = c("i","j")) %>%
  mutate(fdiff = f_i - f_j)

map_dfr(MOD, function(m) map_dfr(FR, function(f) {
  d <- asym %>% filter(model == m, frame == f)
  if (nrow(d) < 10) return(tibble())
  fit <- lm(delta ~ fdiff, d)
  tibble(Model = m, Frame = f, n = nrow(d), `slope on (f_i - f_j)` = coef(fit)[[2]],
         t = summary(fit)$coefficients[2,3], `r` = cor(d$delta, d$fdiff),
         `SD(Δ)` = sd(d$delta))
})) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.,3))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "T3: out-of-sample validation of the Report VI prominence scale. Negative slope = predicted direction.")

         `asymmetry ratio` = ratio) %>%

8. Summary figure — where the prominence gradient lives

map_dfr(MOD, function(m) map_dfr(FR, function(f) {
  d <- asym %>% filter(model == m, frame == f)
  if (nrow(d) < 10) return(tibble())
  ct <- cor.test(d$delta, d$fdiff)
  tibble(model = m, frame = factor(f, levels = FR), r = ct$estimate,
         lo = ct$conf.int[1], hi = ct$conf.int[2])
})) %>%
  ggplot(aes(frame, r, colour = model, group = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.08,
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.35), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, position = position_dodge(width = 0.35)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, position = position_dodge(width = 0.35)) +
  labs(title = "The Report VI prominence gradient is largely specific to the conditional frame",
       subtitle = "correlation of the directional asymmetry with the archival prominence difference (95% CI)\nnegative = the direction Tversky's contrast model predicts",
       x = NULL, y = "r(Δ, f_i − f_j)") + theme_judge()

Verdict

The experiment does its job: it separates the two accounts, and it splits the difference between them in a specific and informative way.

1. cond is not an explicit similarity judgment (T4). rgb’s conditional correlates r = 0.60–0.75 with a directly-asked similarity on the very same pairs — substantial, but sharing only about half its variance — and it correlates better with the archival consensus (0.77–0.88) than with sim (0.52–0.74). The high archival correlation doubles as the harness bridge: this collection reproduces rgb’s original, so the cond/sim gap is a frame effect, not a pipeline artefact.

2. The prominence gradient is strongly frame-bound (T3) — the headline. In the conditional frame the archival f predicts the fresh directional asymmetry powerfully and in the predicted direction for every rater (r = −0.34 to −0.70, |t| = 5.6–15.6): Report VI’s scale replicates out-of-sample, on freshly collected data, in the frame it came from, and it does so more strongly in the larger models. In the explicit similarity and difference frames the same predictor is weak and sign-inconsistent (|r| = 0.06–0.24; two of the ten model × frame cells run the wrong way, both non-significant). The gap-block check agrees: cond concentrates asymmetry in the high-prominence-gap block for every rater (1.35–2.93×), while sim does so only for the two larger Gemmas (1.65×) and diff barely at all.

If f were frame-invariant feature salience it should govern similarity and difference judgments about as well as conditionals. It does not — by roughly a factor of three to five in correlation. What Report VI characterized is largely the geometry of a conditional inference, not of a general similarity faculty. That is a point for the deflationary P(j | i) rival, on the test designed to separate them.

3. Non-complementarity is real, and it grows with model scale (T1). sim + diff is not constant, and — the test that matters — the sum moves with the pair’s overlap in four of five raters: gemma3:27b R² = 0.23 (b = 0.67, t = 7.5), qwen2.5:3b R² = 0.16 (t = 6.4), gemma3:12b R² = 0.07 (t = 4.0), llama3.2:3b R² = 0.04 (t = 2.3). Within the Gemma family the effect is monotone in size — 4B 0.007 → 12B 0.071 → 27B 0.233 — with gemma3:4b the lone null. So Tversky & Gati’s human non-complementarity does reproduce here, but as a capability that emerges with scale rather than a universal property of these raters. The predicted richness channel (f_i + f_j) is never significant; the effect runs entirely through overlap, i.e. through common rather than distinctive features.

4. T2 is equivocal. The relative asymmetry is larger in diff than in sim for four of five raters, which is the contrast model’s ordering, but gemma3:12b reverses it and all the margins are small. cond exceeds both frames in every rater — consistent with (2).

What survives from Report VI. Everything estimated on conditional data: the gradient/curl decomposition, the recovered scale and its composition (base rate plus an independent negativity term, no lexical-frequency component), the low-rank shared curl. Test (2) is genuine out-of-sample confirmation of that scale within cond, which is more than Report VI had. What does not survive is calling it Tversky prominence in the general sense. Report VI should be read as a contrast-model account of rgb’s conditional item — where the contrast model does real explanatory work — and not as an account of similarity judgment at large. Result (3) says the contrast model is not simply wrong about these models either: its signature non-additivity is there, and sharpens with scale.

For the readout account this is the thesis in miniature, on the cleanest test available: same adjective pairs, same models, same response format, three questions — and the structure you recover depends on which question you asked. A “similarity readout” and a “conditional-endorsement readout” are not two views of one object, and the gap between them is not noise: it is systematic, replicates across five raters, and varies with scale.

Limits. Five usable raters after the phi4-mini exclusion, one range-restricted and three from one family; 252 pairs; top-1 responses only, because the endpoint’s logprobs could not be trusted (§1) — so there is no distributional channel here, and the soft-evidence treatment this track wants will need a different collection path.
